subtopic: ALLEGED UTTERANCES OF MEMBER FROM ST. LEONARD
ALLEGED UTTERANCES OF MEMBER FROM ST. LEONARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was a time when people got elected on the basis that Heaven was blue, hell was red. It now appears that, as claimed by the Liberal Member for Saint-Leonard (Mr. Gagliano): "God is a Liberal, and his son is a Christian."
Well now, Mr. Speaker, he is lucky that ridicule never killed anyone, otherwise there would be new elections in Saint-Leonard.
It is almost unbelievable that in 1989 people would utter such absurdities in order to get votes, and that hundreds of Liberals would pay to come and hear them.
At any rate, Mr. Speaker, if the Liberals now believe that God is a Liberal and his son is a Christian, well let the son come to the House of Commons and we will see to it that he drops down into hell!

Mr. Speaker, on June 23, 1985, 329 innocent civilians, mostly Canadians, lost their lives as a result of a terrorist bomb explosion aboard flight 182 from Montreal to Bombay via London.
Extensive media research prominently broadcast on TV and radio has shown that this heinous crime was preventable. There were eight warnings, including a test
explosion that pointed to this impending disaster. Yet nothing was done.
Even though an official Indian government inquiry decided that a bomb had been placed on board, Canada has refused to address this matter.
Canadians have been clamouring for a public inquiry. Within the cities of Ottawa and Nepean, 700 friends and relatives of victims have signed a petition for an inquiry.
Last year, an identical terrorist bombing destroyed a Pan American passenger jet in Britain. Recommendations from the Canadian investigation could have averted this additional tragedy.
It is high time this government began the task of looking into this disaster. I strongly call upon Parliament to give Canadians a commitment to hold a royal commission of inquiry into all facts surrounding the Air India disaster of 1985.
This government should get out from under its rock and begin to take some responsibility to prevent these atrocities from ever occurring again.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the member for South Shore gets up in the House from time to time to claim that his riding has the biggest, fattest lobsters and the biggest, greenest Christmas trees in the whole world.
I would like to take exception to that. In any case, lobsters and Christmas trees are one thing, but there can be no doubt about blueberries. My riding has the biggest blueberries in the country. In fact, we have the biggest pickers, the best producers, the best processors and the largest shippers of fresh blueberries.
The industry is well organized and at the leading edge of technology in this field, but requires some assistance from two areas of the federal government. First, the Day Haul Program from Canada Employment has been crucial to their industry. I urge the minister to maintain this program.

The producers need help in research, development and insect control. I will be asking for help from the appropriate departments in this regard.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the CBC's decision not to broadcast the public affairs radio program Ontario 30 on CBOF-Ottawa any longer is unacceptable. In so doing, the Crown corporation proves that it is indifferent to Ontario's Frenchspeaking community.
Ontario 30 was a link between the various French communities in Ontario. In fact, it was the only French media program to cover all of Ontario. This management decision to end Ontario 30 in Ottawa, the national capital, is one that I regret. It will only further isolate Ontario's francophones. I therefore ask the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse)-and I see his Parliamentary Secretary here today-to intervene with the CBC on our behalf, to show that the CBC really meets the needs of the French-speaking minorities outside Quebec.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to urge all members of the House and, indeed, all Canadians to acknowledge and lend their support in the recognition of National Bums Awareness Week.
Bum injuries are one of the leading causes of accidental death in Canada. Children, the elderly and disabled Canadians are the most likely to suffer severe bums. Many could be prevented by the use of smoke detectors, home escape plans and generally through increased public awareness and proper education.
For example, the execution of the "stop, drop and roll" procedure can mean the difference between a minor injury and a fatal one.
The Shriners of North America and the Canadian Association of Fire Chiefs have addressed this problem,
and through their efforts, the week of February 4 to 10, beginning in 1990, is being recognized as National Bums Awareness Week.
I commend the efforts of these organizations to all Canadians and strongly urge that they support their work. I also know that the appropriate ministers, in particular, will want to lend their support in recognition of National Burns Awareness Week.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to remind all members that this House endorsed unanimously a resolution on September 12, 1983 condemning the Soviet Union for its attack on a Korean civil airliner and the resultant death of 269 innocent people.
To date, there has been no apology or compensation forthcoming to the 10 Canadian families who lost loved ones in this incident, despite the passage of six years.
Given the fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has stated with some regularity a consistent position, and I quote from a letter of September 29, 1988, "Canada continues to hold the Soviet Union liable for damages resulting from the downing of KAL-007", I would encourage the Prime Minister to raise this issue with Mr. Gorbachev in his upcoming visit to the Soviet Union. I would ask that the Prime Minister take this opportunity to seek a formal apology and appropriate compensation.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I had the pleasure of taking part in the opening of the new hypertension unit at the Ottawa Civic Hospital. This revolutionary unit is designed to investigate the causes and treatment of hypertension, a major cause of disability and death in Canadians.
The unit was established through the co-operation of the hospital, government and private participants, and members of the medical community. Major funding was obtained from Sandoz pharmaceutical company as a direct result of Bill C-22, the Drug Patent Act.
November 8, 1989

This is only one example of the millions of dollars being put into medical research in Canada by the pharmaceutical companies, as promised by them as a result of Bill C-22.
This success story will be repeated all over Canada due to the foresight of this government in passing strong and progressive legislation such as the Drug Patent Act.

Mr. Speaker, at tomorrow's First Ministers' Conference the leaders of the Yukon and Northwest Territories governments will have official observer status. Despite requests from the territorial governments for full participant status, the federal government has not seen fit to give northerners the voice they are entitled to at these national conferences.
In a media interview in Yellowknife in September, 1988, the Prime Minister committed himself to working on a formula that would allow the territorial leaders and territorial ministers, and I quote:
-better input in the decision-making process, better presence, better chance to speak out on behalf of the territories and people in the territories.
In the 14 months since the Prime Minister made that commitment we have seen no progress on the status of the territorial government leaders at First Ministers' Conferences.
Simply having the right to make an opening statement is not good enough for the territorial leaders. It is not good enough for the people of the north who see their democratically-elected leaders shut out of the room during subsequent discussions.
This government continues to deny northerners their right to be represented in these critical national discussions which affect them in all areas whether constitutional or economic.
I urge the Prime Minister to take the concerns of the people of the north seriously and allow the two leaders of the two territories to take part in all discussions of the first ministers, as he indicated he would in September, 1988, in Yellowknife.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday we heard that the cabinet of the German Democratic Republic resigned and issued a call for democratic elections of a ruling body.
This occurs following the growing exodus of people from East Germany.
By their actions yesterday, the leaders of East Germany are responding to the will of their people. We applaud the actions of East German leaders and hope that genuine steps to democracy, so well illustrated in the last week, continue in the German Democratic Republic, and that true democratic reform is peacefully accomplished in that country.

Mr. Speaker, the so-called DND environmental impact statement regarding NATO flights over Innu territory completely, and one would have to assume deliberately, ignore the devastating impact these flights have on the Innu people.
This morning the Innu filed a legal action against the Government of Canada in order to stop the low level flights and prevent the establishment of a NATO base in Nitassinan. That the Innu should have to resort to this to see their rights protected is a sad statement indeed.
The Canadian government is wasting an enormous amount of money and time trying to justify the unjustifiable. Not only does its proposed base threaten the Innu people, it also represents part of NATO's FOFA strategy which is now more irrelevant than ever, given the changes taking place in Europe. Instead the government should put its efforts and resources into responding imaginatively to Soviet initiatives in Arctic security.
Gorbachev's Murmansk proposal continues to go unanswered. It is time the Prime Minister woke up and responded in a concrete and positive way. Let us see that happen when the Prime Minister visits the Soviet Union later this month.
Canada is uniquely situated geo-politically to promote disarmament in the Arctic. Let us take up our responsibility and develop policies based on common security principles rather than on confrontation and threat. Let

us end the destructive and senseless flights over Innu land.

Mr. Speaker, the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe met on the environment and just concluded its work in Sophia. Thirty-four of the 35 delegations attending agreed to a plan of action on the transboundary effects of industrial accidents, the management of hazardous wastes, and the protection and use of transboundary watercourses and international lakes.
Pollution in the Canadian Arctic and its sources in Europe was raised, but it was unfortunate that Ottawa did not instruct the Canadian delegation to use this international forum to raise as well North American transboundaiy issues, namely, acid rain and transboun-daiy air pollutants that damage ecosystems and economies. We missed an opportunity to send a strong signal to the U.S., through the U.S. delegation in Sophia.
Transboundary issues remain a high priority on our bilateral agenda, but we also must take every opportunity to raise our concerns in multilateral fora where the environment is on the agenda. We urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs not to let such opportunities slip by in future.

Mr. Speaker, a successful Alberta economy depends on a successful energy industry. Oil and gas development accounts for hundreds of thousands of jobs.
In the riding of Elk Island this influence is demonstrated by the presence of the Strathcona refineries. The energy industry depends on export markets. The Pacific Rim market is an important market for Alberta energy. We must continue to supply this crucial market through dependable and environmentally safe marine tanker shipments.
Let us work together to support Alberta's energy sector. Let us work together to build a stronger economy in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Toronto Labour Council, the Toronto Action Committee on the Status of Women, the Toronto Social Planning Council, Coalition of Visible Minorities and Immigrant Women have recently produced a study on the economic and working conditions that presently exist in the city of Toronto. They have found that these conditions are changing dramatically.
Increased part-time work, temporary work and shift work has meant decreased wages and benefits and less job security for many workers. They also found that in the last three months alone plant closings have cost some 2,500 jobs in the city of Toronto. This study also found that Toronto has a generation of young people who are growing up in the city and who may never be able to live there.
This government should be setting an example as well by initiating programs that will offset the devastating impact of the free trade agreement, cutbacks to VIA Rail, slashing of unemployment insurance programs, and if they get away with it, the GST.
Rather than being a part of the solution, this government is creating the problem. It is high time it began acting in the best interests of Canadian families, rather than big business friends.

Mr. Speaker, in an interview last night on the television program The Fifth Estate, the Minister of Finance was asked about the position of the provinces on his goods and services tax.
This is what the minister said of the provincial positions, and I cite him from the transcript: "They've agreed. Behind closed doors they'll say, ' you got to go ahead with this, Mike'. No question of that".
November 8, 1989

I would like to give the minister an opportunity to back that statement up. I invite him to give the House of Commons the names of the premiers who agree with his version of the goods and services tax. If there are any, why has he not given the House those names before?
speakername: Right Hon. John N. Timer@Leader of the Opposition

speechtext: I am glad the hon. member is watching my performances on television.
Hear, hear!

I was referring in my response to a question put to me by Mr. Mailing, whereby I indicated that we had been discussing with the provincial financial ministers for some two years the design of the goods and services tax. At that point we hadn't called it a goods and services tax, but it is essentially the same structure that was being discussed during the meetings.
One finance minister made it quite clear that he disagreed with a consumption tax, and that is Alberta. It does not have one. I think it is quite clear why it has taken that position.
During the course of these meetings with the finance ministers they were quite in agreement with the fact that we had to change the federal sales tax, for reasons that I have expressed in this House on a number of occasions. During that period of time none of them were saying we should not be changing this FST into something like the goods and services tax.
I want to tell the minister that I watched him last night because I like sitcoms.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, just before the opening of the important First Ministers' Conference, the Minister of Finance accused the provincial premiers of hypocrisy.

speechtext: I dare say we could do something to put the ratings up around here. I will let the hon. minister do that.

Mr. Speaker, I do the best I can.
I think I have responded to that question. We have on many occasions sat down with the provincial finance ministers, as well as the officials. Their need is not as great as ours in terms of reforming the sales tax system.
We have a sales tax that penalizes our exports, that provides imports with a one-third tax advantage relative to Canadian producers. The existing tax is prone to considerable tax avoidance.
If I asked the hon. member, would he be in support of keeping that sales tax in place, I am sure that if he were objective-possibly he will be after December 31-he would say, "Absolutely not, Mike, you had better get on with changing it as well".

Mr. Speaker, those answers of the minister have already cost us half our ratings in the House of Commons.

November 8, 1989

My final question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. He looks as if he wants to participate in some constructive way.
All the premiers to whom I have spoken have told me something quite different from the statements made last evening by the Minister of Finance. They have told me that the Minister of Finance never, ever discussed with his provincial counterparts a formal proposal for provincial participation in the goods and services tax.
Does the Prime Minister intend to put such a proposal on the table at the First Ministers' Conference? Or is he content to move ahead with a proposal that will see Canada as the only country in the world with 10 separate retail sales taxes?

Mr. Speaker, if we continue with this federal sales tax, we will be the only country in the world that has a manufacturers' sales tax. We will be the only country in the world that through its tax system will deliberately tax exports to a greater extent than others and-
Oh, come on, Mike.

Mr. Speaker, I ask the Leader of the Opposition to have some patience for the answer. We would be the only country in the world that penalizes our exports in the way that this tax does. We would be the only country in the world that gives our imports a tax advantage relative-
Name one premier.

I thought I responded to that question in my first answer.
What I said in my first answer was that there was one finance minister who has said all along that he was not in favour. At no time did the other finance ministers say that they disagree with the fact that, (a) we have to change from the existing tax and (b) that the proposal that we had on the table, the national sales tax, the basic structure of which has been repeated in the goods and services tax, is the right way to go.
It was quite clear to me that they did not have the sense of urgency, the need to replace their sales taxes. That is why we decided to move forward with the goods and services tax that we believe is absolutely the right way to go for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance is of course aware there will be a very important conference on the economy on Thursday and Friday this week. We all know about the tensions that exist in this respect.
My question to the Minister of Finance is this: Considering the importance of this conference, and it is common knowledge that all the provinces are opposed to his proposals on the GST, is the Minister prepared to contribute towards a sensible and honourable dialogue with his provincial colleagues by withdrawing the proposed GST?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know what the hon. member refers to or believes is healthy. I think that the approach that we are taking to bring in a goods and services tax is a clear way to improve the health of this economy. That is precisely the reason we are going ahead with it.
I have made it quite clear that if the premiers or the finance ministers, supported by the premiers, can agree on a specific proposal, yes we are prepared to sit down and discuss that with them.
At the August meeting of the premiers and made no attempt whatsoever to even consider alternatives.

Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the government plans to go ahead no matter what. I would ask the finance minister to comment again on his statement last night when he said in response to a question, "There's basically one exemption and that's groceries".
My question to the Minister of Finance today is this. Is he prepared to commit on behalf of his government that when the Conservative majority in this House rams through the GST against the will of the premiers, against the will of Canadians, that his government will not impose a tax either on groceries or existing housing because there are a few other exemptions?

Mr. Speaker, that is a continuation of the line of questioning that he and his colleagues have been using since September of this year.
November 8, 1989

I have made it very clear that I am not going to make statements that are going to preclude the attention and the considerations that the finance committee is going to be having, the finance committee of which he is a member.
We have indicated that we want to listen to what the finance committee has to say and draw our conclusions accordingly. But clearly, the proposal that is on the table to which we have indicated a very strong attachment, does not provide for either of those two things in its make-up.

Mr. Speaker, my question, too is to the Minister of Finance.
The Minister of Finance knows, without exception, all the premiers have opposed the tax.

speechtext: What have they proposed?

He knows also that there is Joe going again. Calm down over there, Joe. I hope our foreign policy is in better control, Your Honour.
Since the First Ministers are here in town, and since the Government of Canada and the premiers ought to obtain maximum co-operation on such a matter, I want to ask the minister this, considering that he said: "Behind closed doors, they'll say, 'You got to go ahead with this'. No question of that. With reference to the tax, they do not want to share the heat, they want to come in later." Will the minister either tell the House of Commons and the people of Canada the name of one premier who said that, or do the right thing and withdraw his comment entirely?

I think that I have responded to that question in response to the Leader of the Opposition. In those comments on the TV program that was aired last night I was referring to the fact that the finance ministers, federal and provincial, had sat around the table for two years discussing a proposal on sales tax reform, which is the same structure as the goods and services tax. The goods and services tax is a federal only proposal. The other proposal, a national sales tax, is federal-provincial, but all the other elements are essentially the same as what we have been discussing with the provinces.
Oral Questions
With the exception of one finance minister, at no time did others say: "Look, we had better stop discussing this". It became quite clear in the way the discussion was going that we were not going to reach a resolution of this; that there was not the need on the part of the provinces to change their sales tax. There was a very clear need on the part of the federal government. That is why we decided to proceed as we have.

Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding what the minister has said, he still has not answered the question. It is a very serious accusation, I say to the minister, to tell the people of Canada that all the premiers are systematically misleading the public. The premiers have come out strongly with the large majority of Canadians in opposition to the tax. The Minister of Finance has said, and these are his words: "You got to go ahead with this".
Can he name one minister of finance or one premier and, if so, which province, has told him to go ahead with it? Who is saying that in private, but is saying something contrary to the people of Canada? As Minister of Finance, he has a reputation to uphold, and if he is going to hurl abuse at the premiers, he has got to document that.

Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear in the context of this that what I was referring to is the fact that we have to go ahead with the replacement of the existing federal sales tax to the goods and services tax. That is precisely the position that the New Democratic Party is stating, and you have said on many occasions-
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party is shaking his head. I can show different occasions on which his party, people speaking on behalf of his party, his finance critic from the last Parliament-
Which premier, Mike?

-was saying that it is important. The member from Regina as well is saying that the existing federal sales tax is a mess, it must be changed, and on this basis we have got to get on with it.
People have been talking about making a change in this tax for 50 years. This is a government that is going to get on with that job.

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, last night the Minister of Finance said that Canada's provincial Premiers had expressed their support for the concept of a GST, but he refuses to repeat that statement here in the House of Commons. The Minister of Finance should speak frankly and honestly here in the House of Commons and before all Canadians. I repeat: Will the Minister of Finance name one Premier who agrees with him on this issue? If he cannot, he should say so and withdraw his comments immediately.

Mr. Speaker, I think the context is quite clear in the program that was aired last night that I was referring to the provinces and, in particular, the meetings that I have been having with the finance ministers. I will be quite precise with the finance ministers and with my comments about the finance ministers.
One finance minister has said that he absolutely disagrees with sales taxes and that is quite clear. It is the province of Alberta. It has made that known publicly on many occasions. But for two years I sat at the table with other provinces represented by their finance ministers and at no time did people say that we should stop talking about this.
Did they say go ahead with it?
They agreed with the fact that we had to go ahead with the change from the federal sales tax to something like the goods and services tax and that is precisely what we are doing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. We are wondering what can be made of the about-face of the Prime Minister on the Cogger affair that, to quote him, it was both forthcoming and proper for the Senate to hold hearings, and forthcoming and proper for the Senate not to hold them, both statements having been made after it became clear that the RCMP was seized of the matter.
My question for the Deputy Prime Minister is, bearing in mind that there were valid concerns about the conduct
of departments and agencies in relation to Senator Cogger, as well as things done by the senator which may not amount to criminal activity but which are nonetheless unacceptable and worthy of being examined by the Senate, will the government not agree that the Senate should proceed to do its work and to do it in its own time frame?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, far be it from me to make a decision in the other place. I am sure that they can make their decisions on their own, and as they will.
I remind the hon. member that there is an RCMP investigation into this. It was the senator himself who asked for the Senate to set up a proper mechanism to hear this particular issue and it will decide in a normal manner. I am not sure what is so bothersome to the hon. member about that process.

I am glad to hear that the government is prepared to recognize the responsibility of the Senate in the matter and for its own timing.
Let me ask the Deputy Prime Minister-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am having a little difficulty understanding on what basis the hon. member is asking the government in this place about what the Senate is or is not doing. It may be a very interesting inquiry, and often is, but I do not know that it has anything to do with the administration of government. I will hear the hon. member's question.

The Senate has a representative in the cabinet who has taken a position on this matter on behalf of the government. I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister, in the light of what I gather is another flip-flop today from what the Prime Minister was saying yesterday, will the government instruct its minister, the Government Leader in the Senate, not to take a position against the Senate holding hearings and holding hearings in its own time frame?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Sir, I am sure the Government Leader in the Senate will act in accordance with the customary practices that are normal. I really find it quite strange that the hon. member is troubled by this.
The opposition raised this issue on the floor of the House, action has been taken, they are still not satisfied. What more do they want?
November 8, 1989

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Employment. Yesterday, four respected social agencies from metropolitan Toronto, the Metro Labour Council, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, the Social Planning Council and the Coalition of Visible Minorities and Immigrant Women released a report to the Toronto city council calling for a city agency to address the growth of part-time jobs at the expense of full-time jobs, the growth of unemployment and to meet the need for job adjustment programs.
Given that these needs are the direct outcome of her government's policies, why is the minister ignoring these deplorable conditions in metro Toronto, and why does she remain inactive in the face of worsening social economic conditions in Toronto?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member, as usual, is way off base.
The government firmly believes-and I think he should listen to this-that the best response to poverty is two-fold. First is the creation of jobs that people can have to work at, and I remind him that the unemployment rate in Toronto is as low as it has ever been. The second is the training and the ability for people to take those jobs.
That is what we are doing through our labour force strategy and the Canadian Jobs Strategy where we have targeted particularly people in need. Through the programs that we have for people on social assistance, which was a program of this government, that is directed at those people who have the most needs.
It is our job as a government, and the member's job as a representative of the people of Toronto, to stand up in this House and say yes, that is what we need, and that is what is happening.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the minister that as a former educator I long ago learned the art of listening. It is something that she might have done because if she had learned to listen she would have heard some of the horror stories about the outcome of her UI legislation. In fact, the economic regions outlined
Oral Questions
yesterday are going to make matters worse for the unemployed, particularly in major centres like Montreal and Toronto.
In view of the fact that there are over 74,000 unemployed in the city of Toronto, that there has been a job loss of over 2,400 full-time jobs in the course of the last three months alone, and that there are over 80,000 persons swelling the ranks of those who depend on food banks in the City of Toronto, largely as a result of her government's policies, and in view of the fact that the social planning council has already predicted an increase of over $10 million in costs on the welfare rolls, what steps will the minister take to discharge her responsibilities to the residents of Toronto, or is she content to shift the burden on to the municipalities that cannot afford to play the role that rightly belongs to her and her government?

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
I would like to remind the hon. member of two things. First, in terms of the social assistance that is provided through municipalities, as he knows, 50 per cent is paid by the federal government. It is not in our interest, nor would we want to increase those numbers.
Second, I ran for public office in the city of Toronto because of the state the economy was driven to by the party that he represents when people in Toronto were forced to sell their houses, when they lost their businesses, when they lost their jobs-
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. I have with me today an economic analysis by the Tourism Industry Association of Canada regarding the impact of the proposed goods and services tax.
The analysis states that under the proposed goods and services tax, tourism is slated to lose $1.2 billion a year and at least 30,000 Canadian jobs. Another analysis by the Tourism Research Institute of Canada states that under stage two the GST will lower employment in the service sector by 48,000 jobs. A third report by the hotel

industry of British Columbia indicates a deterioration in the travel deficit by about $348 million.
My question to the Minister of Finance is in relation to the evidence in front of him. How can the minister say that these tax measures are good for Canada when at least-I say at least- 30,000 tourism jobs are on the line and there will be an economic loss in tourism activity of over $2 billion?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member, I regret to say, has got his figures wrong. The report that he is quoting states that the phenomenal rate of growth of tourism in this country will level off somewhat briefly but it will continue. Therefore, the job losses that he is suggesting are totally fictional.
The second thing is that western Canada above all is experiencing an absolute boom in tourism in Alberta, British Columbia and the prairies. Through the operation of the GST we are now going to be giving input tax credits, something the industry has never had before. They pay the 13.5 per cent, do not get a tax credit back for it, so the costs of doing business will go down. Plus, we are bring 4,000 travel agents from all over Europe to see western Canada in about three month's time.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has in fact confirmed that the jobs that could have been produced without the GST will not be produced with the GST. He has in fact confirmed that Canada's $2 billion a year travel deficit will now increase by another $348 million a year.
Question?
Sorry, my question to the minister- Mr. Speaker, I was wrapped up in my statement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: So was I. The hon. member will put his question.

Thank you for the latitude, Mr. Speaker, I was so involved in the statement that I forgot the question.
My question to the minister is, does he not recognize that in fact that $348 million additional loss in Canada's trade deficit is going to increase the over-all trade deficit that Canada now experiences of some $2 billion a year?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no, I will not agree with that. I will tell the hon. member that when he asks a question again to make sure that he reads the conference report very carefully, and that he make sure he reads the amendments to the original report that have been done giving the exemptions we have put in place.
We are exempting foreign tourists from the GST on accommodation and on products that they buy. We are the only country with a GST that will exempt accommodation.

Mr. Speaker, although we on this side of the House are very pleased that Mrs. Aquino leaves this country with a firm commitment from the Canadian Government for assistance totalling $125 million and also that she found the time to lay a wreath at the Cenotaph, we wonder, now that we are getting ready to welcome Mr. Lech Walesa to Ottawa, whether the government is prepared to do as much for Poland as it did for the Philippines, considering that so far, countries like Germany and France have been far more generous to Poland than the Canadian Goverment has been.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada has co-operated with other countries, thereby showing a profound interest in the changes that are taking place in Poland and also in Hungary. We want to make a substantial contribution to these reforms and do so financially, but also by offering Canadian aid and expertise, in order to promote development in that part of the world. We are considering other ways in which Canada could continue to play an important part in Poland's growing reforms. Here in Canada, we have a number of Canadian citizens of Polish origin who are in a very good position to establish close links between Canada and Poland. This is a very important moment in our history.

Mr. Speaker, I want to remind the minister that obviously words are important but actions are even more important.
November 8, 1989

Does the minister realize that indeed Poland needs food and more money now. Will the government ensure that food will reach Poland in time for Christmas? Will the government revisit the very modest offer to Poland of a possible $20 million revolving credit to be negotiated within a very strict time frame and contingent upon an agreement with the International Monetary Fund?
Can we do better, and will we do better?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose one of the realities of the parliamentary system is that any action the government takes will be described as too modest by the opposition. Even allowing that, there is no question that the needs of Poland, and indeed of Hungary, are very great. Canada participated very actively in the discussions flowing from the meeting with the Group of 7 in Paris. We have made an announcement of some of the aid that will be available from Canada, both financial aid and aid in expertise in other ways, and the question of rescheduling, as my colleague indicates.
The question is whether we are prepared to consider, along with the rest of the world, doing more. The answer of course is yes. We are prepared to consider that. We will be ensuring that the activities that Canada takes will be in conjunction with other countries interested in encouraging solid, permanent reforms in Poland.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. Employees of Correctional Service Canada have been on strike since October 30.1 may add that they have had no wage increases since the end of 1986 and that their collective agreement expired in December 1987.
Mr. Speaker, this strike threatens the safety of employees who work in detention centres as well as the safety of inmates and the safety of the public, and it is particularly disturbing for Canadians and Members of this House who have detention centres in their ridings.
Oral Questions
This morning, Mr. Speaker, we heard that the parties had resumed negotiations. Could the President of the Treasury Board inform the House today about what he intends to do to keep the parties at the negotiating table so that a settlement can be reached as soon as possible?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said last Friday in the House, the government has always been willing to return to the negotiating table. In fact, following discussions we had with the unions, an agreement was reached to return to the table as of 2 p.m. today.
Mr. Speaker, I think concrete offers may be discussed at the negotiating table, and without wishing to prejudge events, I may say we are confident that the dispute, which has been going on for more than 10 days, will be setttled in a matter of hours.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. I would like to ask the minister about one tragic aspect of VIA Rail's cut-backs, the impact on Canada's disabled community.
The minister knows full well that many disabled Canadians have no other form of transportation. Buses are inaccessible, air travel is too expensive. I am sure that members opposite know about that. In the face of this, the minister lays off key personnel and cuts back services and routes.
Is this the response that the minister has to the transportation difficulties faced by Canada's disabled community?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague should know that we continue to provide services across the country, from Vancouver to Halifax. VIA Rail services will be provided, particularly in the corridor, with frequency where there are the most disabled people, and will be as accessible as in the past.
At the same time, the Department of Transport with the bus industry is investigating new buses and bus

Oral Questions
services which will also provide to the handicapped people facilities that they did not have in the past.
I understand that in the routes which have been cut, it will perhaps be more difficult, but I also know that the handicapped people understand that the finances of this country have to be managed and they agree with what the government has done with VIA Rail cuts.
Mr. Speaker, I must question the sincerity of the minister. More than a year after Parliament-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I know the hon. member probably did not mean what he said, but one does not here question the sincerity of other hon. members. I know he will want to put his question.
Withdraw.

Mr. Speaker, I withdraw. But the facts remain, unfortunately, for the minister.
The disabled get nothing but inaction from this government. More than a year after Parliament amended the National Transportation Act to enhance accessibility of federally regulated transportation to the disabled, the National Transportation Agency has still not acted to put these amendments into effect.
Why has the minister not urged the National Transportation Agency to act on this legislation, or did the minister intentionally remain silent so as to give VIA Rail false grounds to cut personnel service for disabled Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I hope that my friend knows that the National Transportation Agency is a body independent of the minister. They can make the decision and they can apply their decision. Perhaps it was a fact when the hon. member's party was in in power, but it is not a fact on this side of the House to overrule what is done by the National Transportation Agency.
I want to say very sincerely to my friend that I was Secretary of State for two years and today it is true that with the present Secretary of State, disabled people have never been as well served as they are today.
[Translation)

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Since so many people are now leaving East Germany to find a new home in West Germany, could the Minister inform the House whether the Government will offer assistance to the West German Government, and if so, how does he intend to proceed?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I just received a request for assistance from the government of the Federal Republic of Germany, asking Canada to provide temporary residence in this country for refugees who have just left the Democratic Republic of Germany. We indicated in our reply that we were willing to help.

I received a request yesterday from the West German government asking if on our military bases in West Germany there might be barracks or other space available to provide temporary housing to aid the West German government in responding to the flow of refugees from East Germany.
After consultation with my colleague, the Minister of National Defence and our commanding officers in Germany, we have replied today, the day after the request, indicating that Canada is prepared to co-operate, prepared to make barracks space and other help available to help the West German government accommodate the refugees from East Germany.

I want to thank them very much.

Hear, hear!
November 8, 1989

My question to the Deputy Prime Minister is why is it then that only the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Transport, along with his colleagues from Quebec, have tried to broaden the understanding of the accord? When will the rest of the cabinet fan out across the country dialoguing with Canadians to inform them that the accord is a good deal for Canadians?

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Atlantic Canadians live in daily fear that declining fish quotas will mean the closure of fish plants and the loss of thousands of jobs for fishermen and fish plant workers. This fear is compounded by the Government's acceptance of the free trade panel ruling allowing American processors access to west coast salmon and herring.
Before accepting this panel ruling, has the Minister obtained a legal analysis from his officials assuring that this ruling cannot be used as a precedent by U.S. processors to obtain similar access to our east coast fish stocks? If so, will he undertake to make this information available to the House?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the hon. member that the panel was struck to inquire into landing regulations which this Government introduced in order to better manage and conserve our west coast salmon and herring stock. As I indicated in this House yesterday, the panel findings upheld Canada's sole jurisdiction in determining management requirements to conserve our west coast salmon and herring stocks. I will expect in time, if that question ever arose, a similar interpretation would be placed on its application with regard to all of Canada's fisheries.

Mr. Speaker, does the Minister of Fisheries seriously expect Atlantic Canadians to believe that American processors in need of scarce raw product will not use this ruling to obtain access to our east coast fish stock under the FTA? Now that his Government has capitulated to the U.S. and accepted this ruling on the west coast, does he actually believe that he will be able to resist pressures on the east coast?

Mr. Speaker, the answer, of course, is yes. We believe that the measures we are taking with regard to our trading relations with other countries, particularly the United States in this case, will guarantee the future security of the Atlantic fishing industry, in fact all of

November 8, 1989

Canada's fishing industry, because our fishing industry is an export-dependent industry. We must therefore play by the fair rules of trade and ensure our own fishermen maximum dollar for their resource by allowing them to trade and to export in a free trade arrangement with the United States.

I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Yesterday in The Netherlands, Canada joined most other industrialized countries in agreeing to stabilize carbon dioxide emissions by the year 2000, even though the Environment Minister is quoted as saying: "We would like to have signed something a little stronger". Also yesterday, the Minister of Energy introduced two bills to approve federal government participation in Hibernia and OSLO, two projects which will produce another 20 to 35 million tonnes a year of carbon dioxide emissions. Will the government establish new programs, such as increased support for fuel ethanol and conservation measures, that would reduce CO2 emissions by an amount equal to the 20 to 35 megatons a year by which Hibernia and OSLO will increase CO2 emissions?

speechtext:

On the question of OSLO and Hibernia, I find it interesting what the hon. member has asked because these bills were tabled yesterday and received first reading. The NDP is opposed to OSLO.
Wrong. Absolutely wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: New Democrats are opposed to OSLO on the basis that it is going to create the difficulties the member mentioned in his question. They are opposed to having energy self-sufficiency. They are opposed to development in Alberta. They are opposed to Hibernia. I guess they want the unemployment in Newfoundland. They do not want the industrial benefits in Newfoundland. I am simply saying, you want all the benefits but you do not want to take any of the responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, a significant number of my constituents involved in the tourist industry are concerned about recent actions affecting their industry, namely environmental restrictions in national parks, cuts to VIA Rail, and the effects of the proposed GST on their highly concentrated service sector industry.
My question is for the Hon. Minister of Finance. Will the minister commission a study which will determine the long-term effects that the GST will have on the tourist industry, especially in western Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to answer my hon. friend's question. First, tourism is probably the most environmentally friendly industry in the country, and sustainable development is usually enhanced by tourism more than by any other industry.
Second, in terms of VIA Rail, we are maintaining the high volume routes in western Canada, and we are also opening an opportunity which was not there before for the private sector to move in to providing passenger rail service for tourists in the future.
In terms of a study, we have had the Conference Board study. We are going to be doing a price-value study. We are also doing a major study of the U.S. market. What it is showing us is that tourism in Alberta, British Columbia in particular, and the west is growing by leaps and bounds and will continue to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. It has been drawn to my attention that there are four hon. members who are today celebrating their twenty-fourth anniversary of their election to this great institution, the House of Commons of Canada. They are the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, the hon. member for Victoria- Haliburton and of course our own hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants, who I know we all agree has added a lot of colour and zest to this institution.
Twenty-four years of service as the people's representative in this place is indeed something to celebrate. Their long-standing service is indeed a tribute to the excellent representation which they have provided to their constituents. Having gone through eight elections, it clearly is a demonstration that they have the confidence of the people whom they represent. I am sure I can speak for all members, I know I speak for the members of our party, when I say that all four hon. members are held in very high regard. They have contributed significantly to this institution. They have debated vigorously. They have defended their interests and the things that they believe in. But most of all, they have defended the interests of their constituents, and that is obviously why they have been sent here to represent their people on eight consecutive occasions.
On behalf of my colleagues in government and the members of the Progressive Conservative Party, I want to extend our sincerest and heartiest congratulations to all four members. It is our hope and our wish that they will continue to be with us for many, many more years and contribute in the excellent way they have in the past.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Official Opposition I am pleased to join in the tribute being paid today to four hon. members of this
House of Commons
House who are celebrating the twenty-fourth anniversary of their first election to the House of Commons.
It is an honour to serve in the House of Commons even for a very limited period, but it is a signal honour to have served as long as the hon. members about whom we are talking way that they have served their constituents, it is a tribute to them for the way they have worked in this House. Their service has obviously been well recognized by their constituents and the applause today indicates how they are held in high regard by members on all sides of this House of Commons.
I am delighted on my own behalf and on behalf of all the members of the Official Opposition to pay tribute to four members of this House who are today celebrating a very important anniversary.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party I rise to join with my colleagues in congratulating the senior members of the House who are continuing to serve their constituents well. I want to say on behalf of my colleagues who have worked with the four members in the past in this Chamber or in committee, we have always respected their hard work and the contribution they have made on behalf of their constituents.
I think it is the case that no matter what the party tendency for votes might be in a particular constituency, for a man or a woman to serve for this period of time in the House of Commons must mean that he or she has brought a particular contribution to that constituency or the member simply would not have been re-elected so many times. I say that as a New Democrat.
As an individual to my two Liberal and Conservative colleagues, let me congratulate them on their past work.
Hear, hear!
I wish them well in the years ahead, but I hope all four will be defeated by a New Democrat in the next election.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for giving me this moment. Prime Minister for his very kind remarks today, as well as the House Leader of the Official Opposition

November 8, 1989
House of Commons
and the Leader of the New Democratic Party. I can say that it was my absolute desire to be a member of this House from the age of 14 years on and I am very, very grateful to the people in the Ottawa Valley riding of Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke who have given me the opportunity to fulfil that desire.
There is more to it than the work in debates and so on that goes on around here. There are some very fine friendships formed. I want to say that I have made some tremendous friendships across the floor of this House, as have my other three colleagues, and we have seen some very fine people come and go from this place. As members of Parliament are raked over the coals from time to time, and almost daily, I suppose, we know among ourselves that there are some very fine people who go through this place and they are here for very dedicated reasons.
I recall very well, 24 years ago today, when I started out to visit all the polls early in the morning. The sun was shining, it was a great fall day, and by three o'clock in the afternoon I had my car in the garage putting on snow tires. Seriously, I simply want to say that there is no challenge and no amount of dedication that is too great on the part of any member of this House. It is our determination and sincerity collectively that we must work toward all good causes, for the future of Canada and on behalf of all Canadians. The more that we recall individually and collectively that we are here to support, promote and assist the people of this nation, the greater this institution will be recognized from coast to coast and from north to south in this country.
I want to thank those people who have been very good friends of all of us in this House. I particularly want to congratulate the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton who represents the riding in which I was born and who represented my father and mother and my family personally over the years.
The hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants has been a very distinguished member of this House and has represented his people well. It has been a great privilege to have known him and to associate with him. Of course, the hon. member for Notre-Dame de-Grace is a very dedicated and hard working person in this House.
Among all these very dedicated people and highly respected members of this House there is no-one greater than the present Speaker of this House of Commons, and I thank you for that.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. W. C. Scott (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to share the sentiments that have been expressed by my colleague. I have enjoyed this place immensely and the friendships that have been created here over the years.
Television was not here when we first arrived. I know that some people watching at home probably wonder what kind of a zoo we were really running here.
But I want to say that when we get behind the curtains and think about the great country we have, and how we are doing something to improve life and the quality of life we have here, of which a great many people throughout the world are very envious, it makes you think it is a pretty sane place here.
It is certainly a pleasure to be here. I represent a riding in the heart of Ontario-I call it the core of Ontario- which the hon. member for Renfrew briefly described a moment ago.
We have a great place to live, we have a great country to be proud of. I wish you all the very best. We will all work for the good of our country, a country that is the envy of the world.
As we pass legislation in this place with this bickering and carrying on, I know it is very, very hard for people watching to understand. But what makes it all great is the spirit and understanding we have here as we work together. It is a pleasure to join with my friends today on this very special occasion. I am proud to be a member of the House of Commons and I am proud of our country.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I was awfully glad that my good friend the Deputy Prime Minister stood because I did not know who was going to stand to recognize us here. We had on these little boutonnieres, and I am not a great flower man. 8, 1965. I am not going to make a long speech but my mommy told me years ago to be prepared. I knew that something might happen today once I got the flower in my lapel. brutal murders in the United States, entered our country, was before our courts and is in our institutions now. speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last time I spoke in this place on the issue before us, I began by saying that I speak on behalf of those women who have been faced with bearing a child not of their choosing. Today, once again, I rise on behalf of those same women.
November 8, 1989

Since I first uttered those words we have had no law in this country regarding abortion. In the view of many women including myself the absence of legislation appeared to respect what I believe, that the judgment of women faced with a difficult decision and their capacity to make a better decision than anyone in this chamber on their behalf was respected in that environment.
In my own mind I have always taken it for granted that as a part of the process of a woman making that decision, she would seek the advice and the consultation that she requires with the father of the child and with her family, or she may choose not to seek it but that she would seek medical advice.
Whatever discussions she chose to have or not to have, ultimately it would be her decision. But as time passed it became clear that the situation for women was not more stable in the absence of legislation but indeed the reverse. Some provincial governments took action against the interests of women. The number and intensity of civil actions increased.
In my earlier speech as well, I reminded the House that I am not a minister of God, I am a minister of the Crown, and I continue to take those responsibilities as a minister of the Crown very seriously. In light of this new situation, what is my responsibility as a legislator, along with that of my cabinet colleagues?
We have heard some discussion in this chamber around when life begins. I pointed out then that society and religion over the centuries have had differing views including such things as that the soul enters an unborn baby boy after 40 days and a girl after 80 days, that the soul enters the unborn child at the time of quickening when the woman feels the foetus moving for the first time. We as parliamentarians are not the ones to determine that, and certainly the woman bearing the child is far better qualified after seeking her own religious counsel.
As a legislator my objective in this process was that we provide a stable legislative framework whereby a woman would have entitlement to the medical services she requires when faced with this profound decision. This required first of all an examination of the federal powers in this regard. They are more limited than I would like.
Government Orders
Under the Canada Health Act, which at first glance to many of us seemed the most appropriate vehicle, the Government of Canada is not in a position to specify abortion as a required service. My colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, has gone into his role and that of the Canada Health Act in some detail, and I will not repeat his arguments. I am sure he would agree that we examined exhaustively this possibility.
Second, if we are to have legislation there will of course be sanctions. What will they be? Many women, including myself, wanted legislation outside the Criminal Code. Once again we had few models. One of them was the Narcotics Act. Even there the sanctions remain criminal sanctions, so where is the advantage to women in that?
Once again, after lengthy discussion our conclusion was that our powers were limited to the Criminal Code. This is not a happy conclusion for me, not by a long way. But what we were able to define was that only the person who induces an abortion outside the law should have sanctions applied. This means that women are protected from the fear of prosecution except under very unusual circumstances and that is an improvement over the former law, albeit a marginal one, for women.
For medical practitioners they are not any more at risk of prosecution than they are under the criminal provisions that guide their behaviour in other aspects of their daily practice. Doctors and others with medical responsibility will in the future, as they have in the past, apply high standards of medical ethics to the role that they are called upon to play.
The thrust of this legislation then is to define abortion as a medical act. Based on a definition of health and wellness, it entitles women to abortion under a wide variety of circumstances. In my view this will assist in providing the stable legislative and societal framework which I was seeking.
Sadly, as a federal government we cannot guarantee access, something that women have been asking us to do. What we have done is ensure, to the extent possible, that provinces take their responsibility in this issue seriously and that they live up to their jurisdictional responsibilities in that regard. For women, this may mean that they must continue to press for the right to choice in other venues. I know that they will do that and I support their efforts.

Government Orders
Let me say to them, as I have had to conclude myself, that we do not live in a country where the public supports a woman's capacity to choose totally without some societal rules. That is certainly true of this chamber. It is also true of the wider nation. I reach this conclusion based on many, many telephone calls and letters and personal conversations over these past months. Out of all those opinions put forward, and there were many variations I would grant, if there was a consensus at all it was that this is a matter for a woman and her doctor.
I would remind the House that when the last motion on this issue was before the Chamber, a few people, including myself, supported an amendment-in fact it was the amendment that I was speaking to at that time-that says that such legislation should prohibit the performance of an abortion except when performed by a qualified medical practitioner.
I would also remind the House that essentially this is what we are being asked to support with this bill with more clarity and therefore, the stability that I seek. Some day perhaps, in a more perfect world, public attitudes and the vehicles through which we must act will respect the sensitivity and judgment of women as I do. That day is not today. I therefore support this bill and participated, as others did, in its authorship. We all approached this with respect and sensitivity.
I would urge those members of this Chamber who want to provide the framework for women, in the world as it is and not in the world as we would like it to be, to find it in their hearts to support this motion. We all in this Chamber hold our principles very high. We are here as parliamentarians to stand up for what we believe, but also to seek consensus and to respect the common will. I know that on an issue of this importance members will seek to do so in a spirit of sensitivity and goodwill.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate how difficult this issue is for the minister. I also appreciate that she spoke almost two years ago in the House. I had the opportunity to go back and read her speech very carefully and I was quite moved by it.
I listened very carefully to what the minister who is responsible for the status of women had to say today. I am pleased that she is here and that she is prepared to take part in the debate.
The minister mentioned that this new criminal legislation will provide a stable legal framework for the women of Canada. My contention is that there is no need for criminal legislation in this area. I do not understand how this is an improvement for women over the situation that we have right now where there is no legislation and, in particular, no criminal legislation. So I ask how this would create a more stable situation than the one that we have right now.
I also listened very carefully when the minister spoke about access. We both recognize that access is a problem and she contends that the problem is with provincial jurisdictions. She has urged women to work in other venues, I think was the way she put it. I know that they will work in those other venues but I think that they will continue to work for access in this venue. There is a variety of legal opinions about the Canada Health Act and the ability of the government to provide for access under the act. Some very prominent lawyers feel that that is, of course, available to the federal government.
I ask in particular for her comments about a stable legal framework and how that is an improvement over the situation now without any criminal legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that what we have in the present situation where we have an absence of legislation, and I have certainly thought about this very carefully, is that with an absence of legislation, with abortion not defined as a medical act, there is more reason for other jurisdictions to say that it does not fall under their jurisdiction to provide a service. I think providing entitlement, as we have, and pronouncing it in the national interest and as the will of Parliament as a medical act gives comfort to women as they seek that access through other jurisdictions. As I have said, I would certainly support them in doing that.

Mr. Speaker, I too rise to thank the minister for taking part in this debate. Further to the comments of the hon. member from New Westminster- Burnaby, now that we have some jurisprudence established as a result of the Chantal Daigle case, and guidelines that would limit court challenges, how does she view us not being faced with many tests in the future,
November 8, 1989

based on the new legislation, which will again drag women through the courts on this issue?

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the past there have been civil actions, both under the old Criminal Code provisions and also in a world in which there was not legislation. We are here to legislate, that is our job as parliamentarians. In fact, we were essentially directed by the court to legislate. Legislation that has the will of Parliament behind it will provide a more stable framework. That stability does come from the two venues that I talked about; first of all, the entitlement that therefore should lead to a position in the provinces whereby access can be provided with the backing of Parliament and, second, although I recognize that there will be civil suits, no doubt, again I think that they will be lessened in an atmosphere when Parliament has spoken as well as the courts.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. minister for her response, although I may not share her view. I would like to ask two questions. One, how will that help the women of Prince Edward Island? Second, yesterday I had the opportunity to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare a question with regard to federal government "interference" in the provinces on the question of access. I asked him if the government would not consider intervention if a whole province refused, for example, to undertake open heart surgery, heart surgery or cancer treatment. The federal government would have something to say under the Health Act. The minister did not choose to answer my specific question. I wonder if this minister could possibly answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not, in any way, try to interfere with the prerogatives of my colleague under the Canada Health Act. I do believe that with the kind of legislation that we are presenting today it will be more difficult for a province, within its own jurisdiction, to justify to the women of that province that it is not prepared to provide access.
Throughout the country now we do see people seeking medical services in other provinces for particular reasons because of the kind of expertise that builds up in particular areas. So, I think that it would be very rare for the Minister of National Health and Welfare to suggest that every province has to provide every medical service
Government Orders
to the ultimate of its sophistication. Our job is to ensure that under the Canada Health Act, we have a universal and accessible system with the principles as outlined in the act.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question. As I read the legislation, it appears to place the onus of responsibility on the doctor. There has been a great deal of concern expressed to me since the legislation was introduced last Friday that under certain circumstances many doctors may feel extremely reluctant to perform that kind of operation on a woman in case of litigation. A young woman may go and see a doctor who happens to hold a pro-life position and the doctor will refuse to perform that operation. That young woman may then go to another doctor who may feel, under another set of circumstances, that such an operation is indeed justified. What happens to that second doctor under these circumstances? Would that not lead to other litigation in the courts and the Chantal Daigle case all over again?

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that that is reaching very hard into the kinds of behaviour that people show. That is why I said in my statement that both women and medical practitioners must exercise their judgment in this case. No one can force a doctor or anyone else to perform an operation that that doctor does not want to perform. That will not change under this legislation. It did not change when there was no law. So if a woman seeks to exercise her choice under the bill that we have presented, then medical practice, which has standards from its own association regarding the performance of any kind of surgery will be there to support the doctor that the woman seeks out.
I would also say that this is not new either. The medical association has established standards of practice. This will give it the legislative framework which essentially supports standards of practice and we have to rely on behaviour and judgment.
I come to this House saying that women have judgment. I believe that doctors have judgment and that they have the capacity and the ability to choose. I have always argued that those are the important reasons to give women choice. I have not altered my opinion. I think

November 8, 1989
Government Orders
that within the legislation we have provided they will be able to do that better than they can without a law.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I get into the substance of the matter, I have to say at the outset that this government has been totally negligent in waiting so long to bring forth this legislation. It has been nearly two years since the Supreme Court of Canada declared the previous law unconstitutional. Since then we have had nothing but procrastination and delay. This government has dillydallied, refusing to face up to its responsibilities and, of course, allowing the type of judicial chaos we had during the summer.
Suddenly the minister is trying to rush it through this House. I want to tell him that we will try to be as constructive as we can, but we do not accept the cavalier attitude that the government has shown towards Parliament in dealing with the issue, nor do I believe the people of Canada appreciate that attitude.

Following the Supreme Court's decision, the Government had promised on many occasions that it would introduce a bill at its earliest convenience, to use the very expression used by Ray Hnatyshyn, the predecessor of the current Minister of Justice, who apparently is in line for the job of next Governor General of Canada. But this Government has produced nothing except, in July 1988, a multiple choice questionnaire which has lead us nowhere.
It has been totally inexcusable for the government to leave this matter on hold for nearly two years. Finally, we have now a bill in a context where all Members can consider the situation very closely.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, we are faced with a very sensitive moral dilemma. It is a dilemma which, on the one hand, has an impact on the life of every individual, and on the other hand, has major social consequences for our country. No woman could decide lightly to have an abortion. A woman could only consider it with a lot of anxiety and suffering as a last recourse solution. There is no one here who would trade places with a woman faced with such a decision. I suggest that for those of us who are not women this situation is just impossible to fanthom. The fact remains that in the real world, thousands of Canadian women must face this decision.

Analysing the situation, there could be no more difficult issue for those of us elected by our constituents than to respond to this issue on a national basis. It is not the responsibility of the legislatures. I do not believe it is primarily the responsibility of the courts. It is the responsibility of members of Parliament.
Within our society there are two diametrically opposite and opposed views on abortion. I can appreciate completely the strength, honesty, and commitment of the convictions of both the pro-life and pro-choice advocates. One group of Canadians believes fundamentally that it is a question of the sanctity of life, the protection of life. The other group believes, also fundamentally, that it is a question of a woman's control over her own body, it is a question of personal liberty and security of her person.
There is no way that these two views can be reconciled philosophically. There is no way these two opposing views can be reconciled theologically or indeed politically. Speaking frankly, we will never reach a consensus on this issue in the House of Commons or in the country. We can reach only an accommodation at best.
So what is our duty here? How do we approach the matter? It is our duty, as legislators, to attempt to find that uneasy accommodation between those two points of view. As I have indicated, in arriving at a judgment, the Liberal caucus members are free to vote as they see fit. This is not a partisan matter and we will not treat it in a partisan fashion.
In a pluralistic society such as we have in Canada, with a separation of church and state, no official religion, with a wide variety of moral views, with a growing variety of cultural traditions, a wide spectrum of religious upbringing, our responsibility as legislators is somehow to seek the common good. Our duty is to seek the best equilibrium we can between the two polarized and competing views on the subject of abortion, between two irreconcilable views on abortion.
I come to the subject with a strong conviction that my duty, and I believe our duty, is not to impose our own beliefs rigidly on the views of others who may strongly disagree. Each of us has the right to his own moral perspective. Each of us has the right to express that view clearly. Each of us has the right to try to convince others
November 8, 1989

of his point of view. On the other hand, each of us has a duty to listen to the other point of view.
I believe, therefore, that as members of Parliament, as legislators, we have the responsibility not only not to impose our personal views on a final legislative decision in this type of community in which we live but not to allow our own personal views, no matter how deeply held, and no matter on which side of the issue they may be, to be the sole criterion by which we judge this legislation. An equally important standard in our pluralistic community must be to evaluate this legislation as to whether or not it is the best available accommodation in moving toward the common good.
I do not believe that the majority of Canadians would agree that we should prohibit all abortions. I do not believe that that is where the country is. On the other hand, I do not believe that the majority of Canadians would agree that we should not exercise some control over abortions, particularly in the later stages of pregnancy as suggested by the Supreme Court of Canada.
I have read the Supreme Court judgment. I have lived with this issue for 20 years. I am willing to admit that this legislation perhaps does not fully respond to the test I have just outlined as set forth by the Supreme Court. There may be better words to describe what we are trying to achieve. By removing the requirement in the earlier legislation for therapeutic abortion committees in accredited hospitals, which the Supreme Court found to be impediments to a woman's rights, I believe that the proposed legislation is a serious effort to find the accommodation necessary to resolve the issue in Parliament. At the very least, it deserves further scrutiny by the committee. That is why I propose to vote to allow it to proceed to committee.
